safetyNote: Do not eat. The German mycological society lists Amanita porphyria among mushrooms associated with gastrointestinal poisoning, including reports after heating. Identification of brown-grey amanitas is difficult and confusion with more dangerous species is possible. If eaten, contact a poison centre promptly.

sections.title: Identification
sections.text: A medium-sized amanita with a silky grey-brown to purple-grey or muted reddish-brown cap, usually about 5–9 cm wide. The cap is often nearly smooth, sometimes with a few grey veil patches; its margin is smooth or only faintly striate. Whitish gills are close and may grey with age or bruising. The stem is pale above the ring and often carries grey-violet chevron-like fibrils below it. A thin grey to grey-violet ring may collapse with age.

sections.title: Base and veil
sections.text: The stem ends in an abrupt rounded bulb, sometimes split lengthwise. Fragile universal-veil remnants commonly form a short collar or rim at the bulb top or cling to the bulb, and may disappear. It should not be expected to have a deep, open sac like that of a death cap. Always excavate and inspect the complete base.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: It forms ectomycorrhiza in coniferous and mixed woodland, often on poor sandy or acidic soil. Fruiting is chiefly in summer and autumn. The flesh is pale, with an odour often compared with raw potato, radish or turnip.

sections.title: Similar species and safety
sections.text: Amanita citrina can resemble it in form and odour but usually differs in cap and ring colour. Amanita pantherina and other brown amanitas also need exclusion. Colour, smell, veil and the entire basal bulb must be considered together. The DGfM reports bufotenin in A. porphyria but also records poisoning after heating; cooking is not a basis for treating it as edible.

sections.title: About the plate
sections.text: The plate shows the intact fruit body, a longitudinal section, the cap from above and the gills from below. Its short volval collar at the rounded bulb, grey-violet ring and fibrillose lower stem are emphasized. This illustration cannot establish the identity of a collected mushroom.
